weeks.title: How We Know the Past
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can we build a trustworthy account of the past when evidence is incomplete or disputed?

vocabulary.primary source: Evidence created during the period being studied.
vocabulary.secondary source: An interpretation produced after the period by someone analyzing evidence.
vocabulary.corroboration: Checking one source against other independent evidence.
vocabulary.contextualization: Placing evidence within the conditions, values, and events of its time.
vocabulary.bias: A preference or perspective that can shape what a source includes or omits.
vocabulary.historical claim: A defensible statement about the past supported by evidence and reasoning.

keyUnderstandings: Historical knowledge is constructed by comparing evidence rather than accepting a single account.
A source can be biased and still be useful when its purpose, audience, and context are examined.
Strong historical claims identify uncertainty and explain why selected evidence is persuasive.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Social studies begins with questions. Historians, geographers, economists, and civic researchers do not simply collect facts; they decide what evidence is relevant, test explanations, and communicate conclusions. Because the past cannot be rerun, every historical account depends on surviving traces such as letters, laws, artifacts, maps, photographs, oral histories, buildings, and statistical records.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Sources were created by people with purposes. A tax register records what officials wanted counted; a speech attempts to persuade; a diary may reveal private experience but only one person’s view. Researchers therefore ask who created a source, for whom, under what conditions, and with what possible limits. These questions do not automatically disqualify a source. They help determine what the source can reliably show.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Corroboration is the practice of comparing sources. Two accounts may agree on the sequence of events while disagreeing about motives. An artifact may confirm that a technology existed but not prove how widely it was used. A historian builds a stronger conclusion by combining different kinds of evidence and explaining contradictions rather than hiding them.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: These habits matter beyond history. Citizens face claims in news reports, campaign messages, social media, advertisements, and artificial-intelligence outputs. The same habits—checking origin, context, evidence, and independent confirmation—help people make responsible decisions in the present.

weeks.title: Geography and Human Systems
weeks.essentialQuestion: How does location shape opportunities, risks, movement, and human choices?

vocabulary.absolute location: A precise position expressed through coordinates or another fixed reference.
vocabulary.relative location: A place described in relation to other places.
vocabulary.scale: The relationship between distance on a map and distance on Earth.
vocabulary.projection: A method of representing Earth’s curved surface on a flat map.
vocabulary.migration: The movement of people from one place to another.
vocabulary.human-environment interaction: The ways people adapt to, depend on, and alter natural systems.

keyUnderstandings: Every map simplifies reality and reflects choices about scale, projection, categories, and purpose.
Human settlement is influenced by water, climate, terrain, resources, transportation, and political boundaries.
Migration usually results from interacting push factors, pull factors, networks, and constraints.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Geography asks where things are, why they are there, and why location matters. Physical features such as rivers, mountain ranges, coastlines, soils, and climate influence travel, food production, disease patterns, and settlement. Human geography examines population, language, religion, political borders, economic activity, and cultural landscapes.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: A map is an argument made with symbols. A political map emphasizes borders; a climate map groups places by long-term weather patterns; a population-density map reveals concentration but may conceal seasonal movement. Projections distort shape, area, distance, or direction because a sphere cannot be flattened without tradeoffs.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Migration evidence includes censuses, passenger lists, oral histories, remittance records, border policies, and settlement maps. Researchers distinguish voluntary and forced migration while recognizing that real decisions may fall between those categories. Family ties and transportation networks can be as important as wages or conflict.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Geographic literacy prevents simplistic explanations. Environment creates possibilities and constraints, but people respond through technology, institutions, culture, and power. Two societies in similar environments may make different choices, and the same project can benefit one group while harming another.

weeks.title: Early Humanity and the Agricultural Revolution
weeks.essentialQuestion: Did agriculture improve human life, or did it exchange some freedoms for new forms of security and inequality?

vocabulary.Paleolithic: The period when humans generally lived by hunting, gathering, and fishing.
vocabulary.Neolithic: The later Stone Age associated in many regions with agriculture and settled communities.
vocabulary.domestication: The long-term process of selecting and managing plants or animals for human use.
vocabulary.specialization: The concentration of labor on particular tasks or skills.
vocabulary.archaeology: The study of past societies through material remains and their contexts.

keyUnderstandings: Homo sapiens originated in Africa and migrated over many generations into diverse environments.
Agriculture developed independently in several regions rather than spreading from a single universal center.
Food surplus supported larger settlements and specialization but also contributed to hierarchy, disease exposure, and conflict.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: For most of human history, people lived in mobile or semi-mobile communities. They used detailed environmental knowledge to gather plants, hunt, fish, manage fire, and move with seasons. Archaeological evidence shows innovation in tools, art, exchange, clothing, and shelter long before farming.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Between roughly 12,000 and 4,000 BCE, communities in several regions increasingly domesticated plants and animals. This process was gradual. Some groups combined cultivation with hunting and gathering for centuries. Farming could support larger populations, yet it also required sustained labor, storage, land claims, and defense.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence

weeks.essentialQuestion: Why did early cities require new systems of law, labor, recordkeeping, and authority?

vocabulary.civilization: A complex society with cities, institutions, specialized labor, and systems of communication.
vocabulary.city-state: A city and its surrounding territory functioning as an independent political unit.
vocabulary.bureaucracy: An administrative system of officials and offices.
vocabulary.cuneiform: A wedge-shaped writing system developed in ancient Mesopotamia.
vocabulary.tribute: Goods, labor, or wealth delivered to a ruler or state.
vocabulary.rule of law: The principle that authority is exercised through known laws rather than arbitrary command.

keyUnderstandings: River valleys supported intensive agriculture but required coordinated labor and management.
Writing and accounting expanded partly because governments and temples needed to track resources and obligations.
Early law codes reveal social priorities and inequalities as well as attempts to regulate conflict.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Some of the earliest large urban societies developed near the Tigris-Euphrates and Nile river systems. Rivers supplied water and fertile soil, but flooding patterns differed. Mesopotamian communities built canals and levees across competing city-states; Egyptian rulers coordinated resources along a long river corridor.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Cities concentrated population, craft production, worship, markets, and political authority. Administrators counted grain, recorded labor, collected taxes or tribute, and organized military and construction projects. Monumental buildings displayed religious and political power while also requiring thousands of coordinated workers.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Law codes such as the collection associated with Hammurabi did not function exactly like a modern statute book. They present cases and penalties that reveal ideas about property, family, commerce, status, and justice. Egyptian administrative records, tomb scenes, and inscriptions provide different kinds of evidence about work and authority.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Early states solved coordination problems but also formalized inequality. Studying them helps students ask enduring civic questions: Who writes laws? Whose interests are protected? How should public works be funded? What makes authority legitimate?

weeks.title: Early Africa, South Asia, East Asia, and the Americas
weeks.regions: Africa, South Asia, East Asia, Americas
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did early societies develop complex urban and political systems in different environments?

vocabulary.urban planning: The deliberate organization of streets, drainage, public spaces, and buildings.
vocabulary.dynasty: A sequence of rulers from the same family or lineage.
vocabulary.mandate of heaven: A Zhou political idea that legitimate rule depended on moral performance.
vocabulary.oracle bone: An inscribed bone or shell used in Shang divination and now studied as written evidence.
vocabulary.monumental architecture: Large public construction expressing religious, political, or social priorities.
vocabulary.cultural diffusion: The movement of ideas, technologies, practices, or beliefs between societies.

keyUnderstandings: Complex societies emerged independently in many regions and should not be treated as copies of one model.
Archaeology is especially important where written evidence is limited, undeciphered, or produced mainly by elites.
Urban design, monuments, and trade goods reveal organization, belief, exchange, and inequality.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Nubia and Kush developed along the Nile south of Egypt and maintained their own political traditions while trading and competing with northern neighbors. Indus cities such as Mohenjo-daro used planned streets, standardized bricks, wells, and drainage. Shang and Zhou rulers in China connected lineage, ritual, warfare, and agricultural authority. Olmec centers in Mesoamerica developed monumental art and regional exchange.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: These societies organized labor in different ways. Some built dense cities; others linked ceremonial centers to farming communities. Rulers used ritual, military power, ancestry, or claims of cosmic order to justify authority. Trade moved metals, stone, crafted goods, and agricultural products across long distances.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Evidence includes city plans, seals, bronze vessels, burials, inscriptions, colossal heads, and environmental data. The Indus script remains undeciphered, so interpretations must rely heavily on material evidence. Oracle bones preserve elite questions but also reveal crops, warfare, weather, and political concerns.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Comparative history is strongest when it identifies both shared challenges and distinctive solutions. Similar monuments do not prove identical governments, and the absence of deciphered writing does not mean a society lacked sophisticated institutions.

dailyLessons.title: Frame the Inquiry
dailyLessons.objective: Locate Early Africa, South Asia, East Asia, and the Americas in time and space and develop an initial answer to the essential question.
dailyLessons.warmup: Without notes, write three observations or questions suggested by the title “Early Africa, South Asia, East Asia, and the Americas.”
dailyLessons.instruction: Nubia and Kush developed along the Nile south of Egypt and maintained their own political traditions while trading and competing with northern neighbors. Indus cities such as Mohenjo-daro used planned streets, standardized bricks, wells, and drainage. Shang and Zhou rulers in China connected lineage, ritual, warfare, and agricultural authority. Olmec centers in Mesoamerica developed monumental art and regional exchange.
dailyLessons.guidedPractice: Build a class chronology for c. 3000–500 BCE and identify the focal region(s): Africa, South Asia, East Asia, Americas. Mark what is known, inferred, or still questioned.
dailyLessons.independentPractice: Complete the first section of the weekly inquiry notebook: initial claim, two questions, and a labeled time-space frame.
dailyLessons.checkForUnderstanding: Explain one way chronology or geography prevents a misleading interpretation.
dailyLessons.support: Provide a partially completed timeline, vocabulary preview, read-aloud option, and sentence frames.
dailyLessons.extension: Identify one periodization choice that another historian might challenge.

dailyLessons.title: Read Like a Historian
dailyLessons.objective: Source, contextualize, and corroborate primary and secondary evidence.
dailyLessons.warmup: Preview the source study: Four Archaeological Case Files. Predict its possible audience and purpose.
dailyLessons.instruction: These societies organized labor in different ways. Some built dense cities; others linked ceremonial centers to farming communities. Rulers used ritual, military power, ancestry, or claims of cosmic order to justify authority. Trade moved metals, stone, crafted goods, and agricultural products across long distances.
dailyLessons.guidedPractice: Analyze an Indus city plan, a Shang bronze, a Kushite monument, and an Olmec sculpture. Infer purpose, labor, and authority while labeling uncertainty.
dailyLessons.independentPractice: Complete Assignment 1, identifying origin, audience, purpose, context, claims, useful evidence, limits, and one corroborating source needed.
dailyLessons.checkForUnderstanding: State one claim the source can support and one claim it cannot support by itself.
dailyLessons.support: Chunk the source, define difficult words, and allow oral annotation before writing.
dailyLessons.extension: Locate a second perspective and explain whether it confirms, complicates, or contradicts the first.

dailyLessons.title: Map and Measure
dailyLessons.objective: Use geographic and quantitative evidence to explain patterns and relationships.
dailyLessons.warmup: Study the map or data before reading its title. List two patterns and one question.
dailyLessons.instruction: Evidence includes city plans, seals, bronze vessels, burials, inscriptions, colossal heads, and environmental data. The Indus script remains undeciphered, so interpretations must rely heavily on material evidence. Oracle bones preserve elite questions but also reveal crops, warfare, weather, and political concerns.
dailyLessons.guidedPractice: Map river systems, resource zones, and exchange routes connecting the four regions.
dailyLessons.independentPractice: Compare evidence of standardization—brick sizes, weights, ritual objects, or artistic conventions—as a sign of coordination.
dailyLessons.checkForUnderstanding: Describe one pattern, one plausible explanation, and one limitation of the map or data.
dailyLessons.support: Provide map labels, a graph-reading guide, and worked example for one calculation.
dailyLessons.extension: Create an alternative visualization and explain what it reveals or hides.

dailyLessons.title: Discuss, Debate, and Write
dailyLessons.objective: Construct an evidence-based argument that acknowledges a competing interpretation.
dailyLessons.warmup: Choose an initial position on: Should historians use the word civilization if it risks ranking societies?
dailyLessons.instruction: Comparative history is strongest when it identifies both shared challenges and distinctive solutions. Similar monuments do not prove identical governments, and the absence of deciphered writing does not mean a society lacked sophisticated institutions.
dailyLessons.guidedPractice: Use a claim-evidence-reasoning organizer. Require evidence from the weekly reading, source study, and map or data lab.
dailyLessons.independentPractice: Complete Assignment 3 as a structured seminar contribution, policy memo, or evidence-based response.
dailyLessons.checkForUnderstanding: Revise the claim after hearing a counterargument and explain what changed.
dailyLessons.support: Offer sentence stems for agreeing, disagreeing, qualifying, and citing evidence.
dailyLessons.extension: Write a counterclaim strong enough that a reasonable person could accept it.

weeks.title: Belief, Ethics, and Philosophy
weeks.regions: Southwest Asia, South Asia, East Asia
weeks.essentialQuestion: How do belief systems answer questions about duty, suffering, justice, identity, and good government?

vocabulary.dharma: A complex South Asian concept involving duty, order, conduct, and right living.
vocabulary.karma: The principle that actions have moral consequences across life and, in many traditions, rebirth.
vocabulary.nirvana: In Buddhism, liberation from craving, suffering, and the cycle of rebirth.
vocabulary.filial piety: Respect and responsibility within family relationships, emphasized in Confucian thought.
vocabulary.ethical tradition: A body of teachings about right conduct, responsibility, and human flourishing.

keyUnderstandings: Religious and philosophical traditions developed in specific historical settings but continued to change across time and place.
Traditions must be studied through multiple voices rather than reduced to one rule or stereotype.
Belief systems influenced law, family, education, art, political legitimacy, and social reform.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Ancient societies developed rich traditions for understanding human purpose and social order. Vedic traditions contributed to diverse forms of Hindu thought. Buddhism emerged in South Asia and examined suffering, desire, ethical conduct, and liberation. Ancient Israelite religion developed a covenantal and ethical monotheism. Confucian and Daoist thinkers responded to political disorder in China with different visions of harmony.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: These traditions shaped institutions as well as personal practice. Ideas about duty, compassion, family responsibility, ritual, justice, and legitimate government affected education and law. Yet no tradition remained uniform. Teachers, communities, rulers, reformers, and ordinary practitioners interpreted ideas differently.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Students should read short, contextualized selections rather than treating sacred or philosophical texts as isolated slogans. A passage’s genre, translation, audience, and historical setting matter. Academic study describes beliefs respectfully without asking students to accept or reject a faith.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Comparing traditions can reveal shared questions without pretending that answers are identical. The purpose is not to rank religions but to understand how ideas travel, change, and influence human choices.

weeks.title: Persia and the Greek World
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did empires and city-states organize citizenship, diversity, military power, and political participation?

vocabulary.satrapy: An administrative province of the Persian Empire.
vocabulary.polis: A Greek city-state and its civic community.
vocabulary.democracy: A system in which political authority is exercised by the people, directly or through representatives.
vocabulary.oligarchy: Rule by a small, privileged group.
vocabulary.citizenship: Legal membership in a political community with defined rights and duties.
vocabulary.historical perspective: Understanding actions and ideas within the conditions of their own time.

keyUnderstandings: The Persian Empire governed a vast, diverse territory through provinces, roads, tribute, and negotiated local autonomy.
Athenian democracy expanded direct participation for male citizens while excluding women, enslaved people, and foreigners.
Greek sources about Persia must be evaluated alongside Persian evidence because wartime rivals often portray one another selectively.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: The Achaemenid Persian Empire connected lands from Central Asia and the Indus Valley to Egypt and Anatolia. Its rulers used provincial administration, roads, messengers, tribute systems, and imperial ceremony. Local languages, religions, and elites often continued under Persian rule as long as taxes and loyalty were maintained.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: The Greek world consisted of many poleis rather than one unified nation. Athens developed direct democratic institutions for a limited citizen body. Sparta organized society around military readiness and an unequal labor system. Rivalry and cooperation shaped wars against Persia and later conflict among Greek states.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Much written evidence comes from Greek authors, especially Herodotus. Their accounts are invaluable but reflect Greek questions and storytelling. Persian royal inscriptions, archaeology, art, and administrative tablets provide different perspectives on imperial rule.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: The comparison challenges a simple freedom-versus-tyranny story. Both Persian and Greek systems combined participation, hierarchy, coercion, and negotiation in different forms.

weeks.dataTask: Compare who had political voice, military obligations, legal protections, and economic duties in Athens, Sparta, and Persia.

weeks.title: Rome and Han China
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did large empires build durable institutions, and why did those institutions eventually weaken or change?

vocabulary.republic: A political system in which public authority is exercised through institutions rather than hereditary monarchy alone.
vocabulary.imperial bureaucracy: A network of officials administering an empire.
vocabulary.civil service: Government administration carried out by appointed or selected officials.
vocabulary.Romanization: The uneven spread and local adaptation of Roman language, law, customs, and institutions.
vocabulary.Silk Roads: Overland and connected trade routes linking East Asia, Central Asia, Southwest Asia, and the Mediterranean.
vocabulary.continuity and change: A historical reasoning process that identifies what persisted and what transformed over time.

keyUnderstandings: Rome and Han China used roads, taxation, military force, law, and local elites to govern large territories.
Both empires promoted political order while incorporating diverse populations through different forms of citizenship and administration.
Their decline involved multiple interacting causes rather than a single collapse event.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Rome grew from a city-state into a republic and then an empire surrounding the Mediterranean. Han China consolidated territories after the Qin and developed an imperial bureaucracy shaped by Confucian learning. Both ruled large populations, collected taxes, built infrastructure, and defended long borders.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Roman institutions included assemblies, magistrates, a senate, provincial governors, and eventually powerful emperors. Citizenship expanded over time. Han government relied on appointed officials, commanderies, household registration, and state involvement in strategic goods. Local families remained important in both systems.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Evidence includes laws, coins, roads, tombs, census records, letters, official histories, and archaeological remains. Comparing evidence shows how imperial policies looked different from the capital than from a frontier village.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Neither empire simply disappeared overnight. Political fragmentation, fiscal strain, warfare, disease, succession crises, migration, and local adaptation changed imperial structures. Later societies continued to use Roman law, Chinese bureaucratic traditions, languages, religions, and infrastructure.

weeks.unit: Unit 3 · Regional Worlds and Expanding Faiths
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did rulers, merchants, and religious communities connect South Asia to a wider oceanic world?

vocabulary.Mauryan Empire: A major South Asian empire founded in the late fourth century BCE.
vocabulary.edict: An official public order or proclamation.
vocabulary.monsoon: A seasonal wind pattern that strongly shapes Indian Ocean travel and rainfall.
vocabulary.diaspora: A community living outside an ancestral homeland while maintaining connections.
vocabulary.stupa: A Buddhist commemorative structure associated with relics and devotion.
vocabulary.decimal place-value system: A numerical system in which a digit’s position determines its value.

keyUnderstandings: Ashoka’s edicts used public inscriptions to communicate moral and administrative expectations across a diverse empire.
Indian Ocean merchants used predictable monsoon winds to connect East Africa, Southwest Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.
South Asian religious, mathematical, literary, and artistic traditions spread through exchange and local adaptation.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: The Mauryan Empire unified much of South Asia through military power, taxation, provincial government, roads, and diplomacy. Emperor Ashoka later sponsored inscriptions presenting an ethic of restraint, welfare, and religious respect after a destructive war. These edicts reveal both political communication and royal self-presentation.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: After Mauryan rule, South Asia remained politically diverse. The Gupta period is often associated with courtly literature, mathematics, astronomy, and temple culture, but achievements involved many regions and communities. Social organization included occupational, kinship, religious, and status groups whose experiences varied.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Indian Ocean navigation depended on seasonal monsoon winds. Merchants carried spices, textiles, ivory, metals, ceramics, and ideas. Ports became multilingual spaces, and religious communities often traveled along commercial routes.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: South Asia was not an isolated civilization bounded by modern borders. Its history demonstrates how land empires, port cities, pastoral zones, and ocean networks interacted.

weeks.essentialQuestion: How did cities, states, and scholarly networks preserve, debate, and create knowledge across regions?

vocabulary.Byzantine Empire: The continuation of the eastern Roman Empire centered on Constantinople.
vocabulary.caliphate: A political community or state led by a caliph in Islamic history.
vocabulary.sharia: A broad Islamic moral and legal tradition derived through interpretation of religious sources.
vocabulary.translation movement: The organized translation and study of works across languages.

keyUnderstandings: Byzantium preserved Roman institutions while developing distinctive Greek-speaking Christian traditions.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Constantinople occupied a strategic position between the Black Sea and Mediterranean. Byzantine rulers used Roman law, taxation, diplomacy, military organization, and Orthodox Christianity to sustain an empire for centuries. Justinian’s legal compilation influenced later legal traditions.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Islam began in seventh-century Arabia. Muslim communities developed religious, legal, political, and intellectual institutions across expanding caliphates. The Umayyad and Abbasid periods differed in capitals, administration, and political coalitions. Non-Muslim communities participated in economic and scholarly life under varied conditions.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Cities such as Baghdad, Cairo, Córdoba, and Constantinople linked libraries, markets, observatories, workshops, and courts. Translation was not passive preservation: scholars tested medical claims, developed algebra, refined astronomy, and debated philosophy.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: This history counters the idea that knowledge belongs to one civilization. Intellectual change often occurs through multilingual exchange, institutional support, criticism, and adaptation.

weeks.unit: Unit 3 · Regional Worlds and Expanding Faiths
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did African states use trade, agriculture, religion, and political organization to build regional power?

vocabulary.trans-Saharan trade: Commercial exchange across the Sahara using caravan routes.
vocabulary.Sahel: The semi-arid transition zone south of the Sahara.
vocabulary.griot: A West African oral historian, musician, and keeper of genealogies and traditions.
vocabulary.Swahili Coast: East African coastal societies linked by Kiswahili language and Indian Ocean trade.
vocabulary.oral tradition: Knowledge transmitted through spoken performance and community memory.
vocabulary.archaeological context: The location and relationships that give an artifact historical meaning.

keyUnderstandings: Africa contained diverse political systems, ecological zones, and trade networks rather than a single historical experience.
Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Great Zimbabwe, Aksum, and Swahili city-states gained power through different combinations of agriculture, trade, tribute, and diplomacy.
Oral traditions and archaeology are essential sources that must be interpreted with methods appropriate to each.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: West African states developed near the Sahel, where farming zones met trans-Saharan caravan routes. Gold, salt, textiles, books, and enslaved people moved through commercial networks. Mali’s rulers used tribute, military power, and alliances, while cities such as Timbuktu became centers of scholarship and trade.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: In eastern and southern Africa, Aksum connected Red Sea commerce, Great Zimbabwe grew through cattle and gold networks, and Swahili cities linked African producers with merchants from Arabia, Persia, India, and beyond. Coastal culture developed locally while incorporating international influences.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Arabic traveler accounts, oral epics, manuscripts, architecture, coins, ceramics, and settlement remains provide different views. Outside observers may misunderstand local customs; oral traditions may combine memory, performance, and political purpose. Corroboration is therefore crucial.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: African history is central to world history. Its states and communities shaped global gold supplies, religious scholarship, ocean trade, agriculture, and diasporic culture.

weeks.title: Medieval Europe
weeks.unit: Unit 3 · Regional Worlds and Expanding Faiths
weeks.essentialQuestion: How were land, labor, religion, law, and political authority negotiated in medieval Europe?

vocabulary.feudalism: A modern label for varied relationships of land, loyalty, and military service in medieval Europe.
vocabulary.manorialism: The organization of rural production around an estate and dependent labor.
vocabulary.serf: A rural laborer legally tied to land under specific obligations.
vocabulary.guild: An association regulating a craft or trade in a town.
vocabulary.Magna Carta: A 1215 English charter limiting certain royal actions and affirming baronial rights.
vocabulary.representative institution: A body in which selected people speak or decide for larger groups.

keyUnderstandings: Medieval Europe was politically fragmented, and historians debate using a single feudal model for diverse regions.
The church was a religious institution, landholder, educator, legal authority, and political actor.
Town growth, commerce, universities, and representative institutions altered older rural and aristocratic arrangements.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: After western Roman authority fragmented, kingdoms, local lords, monasteries, towns, and rural communities developed overlapping forms of power. Landholding and military obligations varied widely. The term feudalism can be useful, but it can also make diverse relationships appear more uniform than they were.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Most people worked in agriculture. Manorial records show rents, labor duties, harvests, disputes, and access to common resources. Towns expanded through craft production and trade. Guilds protected skills and members but also limited entry and competition.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: The Latin church connected communities through worship, law, education, charity, and political influence. Conflicts arose over appointment of officials, taxation, doctrine, and the boundaries between religious and royal authority.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Magna Carta initially addressed a conflict between an English king and powerful barons, not universal democracy. Its later interpretation illustrates how documents can acquire new political meanings over time.

weeks.title: East Asia, 600–1450
weeks.unit: Unit 4 · Connections Across the Medieval World
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did states use education, technology, trade, and cultural borrowing to strengthen authority?

vocabulary.civil-service examination: A competitive system used in imperial China to select some officials through tested learning.
vocabulary.meritocracy: A system that claims to assign status or office based on demonstrated ability.
vocabulary.Neo-Confucianism: A later development of Confucian thought shaped by philosophical and religious debate.
vocabulary.shogunate: A Japanese military government led by a shogun.
vocabulary.tributary relations: Diplomatic and commercial relations expressed through ritual acknowledgment of hierarchy.
vocabulary.commercialization: The expansion of production and exchange for markets.

keyUnderstandings: Tang and Song governments expanded bureaucratic administration and examination culture, though elite families retained advantages.
Printing, gunpowder, navigation, iron production, and commercial growth changed East Asian economies and societies.
Korea and Japan adopted and adapted Chinese institutions rather than simply copying them.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Tang and Song China supported large cities, long-distance trade, tax administration, and educated officials. The examination system offered a route into office but required years of study and resources, so wealthy families remained advantaged. Printing widened access to texts while also strengthening standard curricula.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Commercial growth linked farms, workshops, canals, ports, and markets. Paper money, improved shipping, iron production, and urban consumption supported complex exchange. Technology developed through accumulated experimentation and state, military, and commercial demand.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Korean kingdoms adopted writing, Buddhism, Confucian administration, and technologies while preserving local institutions. In Japan, court culture, landholding, warrior networks, and later shogunates produced a distinct political system.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Cultural borrowing is active selection. Imported ideas change when local societies reinterpret them, and the borrowing society contributes innovations of its own.

weeks.essentialQuestion: How did Indigenous societies build complex governments, knowledge systems, and environmental adaptations?

vocabulary.tribute state: A state that requires subject communities to deliver goods, labor, or military support.
vocabulary.chinampa: A highly productive raised-field farming system used in the Basin of Mexico.
vocabulary.ayllu: An Andean kin-based community with shared obligations and resources.
vocabulary.wayfinding: Navigation through stars, swells, winds, clouds, wildlife, and accumulated knowledge.
vocabulary.oral history: A recorded or transmitted account based on spoken memory and testimony.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Maya cities combined dynastic rule, trade, agriculture, writing, calendrical knowledge, and regional rivalry. The Mexica built a tribute empire centered on Tenochtitlan, a large island city supported by causeways, markets, and chinampa agriculture. The Inca governed a vast Andean territory through roads, storehouses, labor obligations, local officials, and quipu records.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: North American Mississippian societies built urban ceremonial centers such as Cahokia and linked communities through rivers and exchange. Pacific navigators settled islands across enormous distances using wayfinding traditions rooted in observation and teaching.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Evidence includes codices, architecture, earthworks, oral traditions, quipu, ecological records, and colonial accounts. Colonial writers often misunderstood or deliberately recast Indigenous institutions, making source comparison essential.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: These histories demonstrate that complex societies do not require identical technologies or political forms. They also show the continuing presence and knowledge of Indigenous peoples rather than ending their history at European arrival.

weeks.title: Networks of Exchange
weeks.unit: Unit 4 · Connections Across the Medieval World
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did long-distance exchange transform societies far from the merchants who carried the goods?

vocabulary.Silk Roads: Interconnected overland routes across Eurasia rather than one continuous road.
vocabulary.caravanserai: A lodging and exchange site serving merchants and travelers.
vocabulary.merchant diaspora: A trading community living abroad while maintaining commercial and cultural ties.
vocabulary.diffusion: The spread of ideas, technologies, organisms, or practices.
vocabulary.commodity: A good produced or exchanged in a market.

keyUnderstandings: Trade networks depended on many short-distance exchanges, political protections, transport technologies, and credit relationships.
Merchants moved religions, artistic forms, languages, technologies, crops, and diseases as well as luxury goods.
The effects of trade were uneven: port cities and crossroads often changed faster than isolated communities.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: The Silk Roads, Indian Ocean routes, trans-Saharan caravans, and connected regional markets formed overlapping systems. Few merchants traveled from one end of Eurasia to the other. Goods usually passed through many hands, each exchange adding cost and new cultural meaning.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: States taxed and protected trade, while merchant diasporas created trust across distance through family, religious, and linguistic networks. Caravanserais, ports, credit arrangements, and navigational knowledge reduced risk.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Traveler accounts describe unfamiliar customs but often exaggerate wonders. Archaeologists trace ceramics, coins, shipwrecks, textiles, and plant remains. A single object can reveal production, transport, imitation, and consumption across several societies.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Network thinking helps explain how a political change in one region can alter prices or migration elsewhere. It also connects premodern exchange to modern supply chains without assuming they functioned identically.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Steppe societies developed highly mobile pastoral economies adapted to grasslands. Chinggis Khan united rival groups and created disciplined military and administrative systems. Mongol armies used horses, intelligence networks, siege specialists, diplomacy, and terror against divided states.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: The Mongol Empire fragmented into khanates that governed China, Central Asia, Persia, and parts of Eastern Europe differently. Trade and diplomatic movement increased along protected routes, but conquest also caused massive destruction and displacement.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Plague bacteria moved through ecological reservoirs and human networks. Contemporary accounts describe mortality, fear, scapegoating, labor shortages, and religious responses. Exact death rates are uncertain because records are incomplete and uneven.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: The week demonstrates contingency: disease was biological, but its spread and social effects depended on trade, war, inequality, institutions, and human reactions.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Comparison is not a contest to determine which society was most advanced. A useful comparison asks the same question of each case while explaining why differences emerged. It also avoids treating modern nation-states as timeless units.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Students work with a source packet containing laws, traveler accounts, maps, objects, architecture, and quantitative estimates. They practice grouping documents, recognizing point of view, and building a thesis that answers a question rather than listing facts.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Midcourse synthesis strengthens long-term memory and prepares students for the midterm. More importantly, it shows that evidence can support multiple defensible arguments when reasoning is explicit.

vocabulary.Renaissance: A period of cultural and intellectual change associated with renewed engagement with classical traditions.

keyUnderstandings: Renaissance change grew from medieval institutions, Mediterranean exchange, urban wealth, and classical study rather than appearing suddenly.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Renaissance humanists studied Greek and Roman writings to improve education, civic life, and moral judgment. Italian city-states provided wealthy patrons, libraries, courts, and competitive public spaces. Scholars also depended on knowledge transmitted through Byzantine, Islamic, Jewish, and medieval European networks.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Artists used geometry, observation, anatomy, symbolism, and new approaches to perspective. Their works reflected religious devotion, civic pride, family status, political propaganda, and individual creativity. Women participated as patrons, writers, artists, and readers despite institutional barriers.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Movable-type printing made it possible to reproduce many copies more quickly than manuscript production. Printers still faced material costs, censorship, literacy limits, and market risk. Images and pamphlets helped reach audiences beyond university scholars.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Information technology changes who can speak, how quickly ideas travel, and who can control access. The printing revolution offers a useful comparison with digital media without assuming the two are identical.

weeks.essentialQuestion: Why did religious reform become a political, social, and media revolution?

vocabulary.indulgence: In Catholic teaching, a remission of temporal punishment associated with sin; controversial in Reformation debates.
vocabulary.Reformation: Movements that challenged and reshaped western Christianity in the sixteenth century.
vocabulary.Counter-Reformation: Catholic reform and response to Protestant movements.
vocabulary.confessional state: A political order closely identified with a particular religious confession.
vocabulary.toleration: Permission for people to practice beliefs disfavored by authorities.
vocabulary.pamphlet: A short, inexpensive printed work used to inform or persuade.

keyUnderstandings: Reform movements grew from theological disputes, church criticism, political ambitions, printing, and local grievances.
Protestant traditions were diverse, and Catholic reform involved internal renewal as well as opposition.
Religious conflict reshaped state power, education, migration, censorship, and ideas about toleration.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Criticism of church leadership and practice existed before Martin Luther, but printing and political conditions helped his 1517 challenge spread widely. Debates concerned salvation, authority, scripture, ritual, and the organization of the church.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Rulers and city councils often supported or opposed reform for mixed reasons. Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Anabaptist, and other movements differed sharply. Catholic reform included the Council of Trent, new religious orders, education, art, and discipline.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Pamphlets, sermons, songs, images, decrees, and court records reveal how ordinary people encountered reform. Sources may use hostile labels and exaggerate opponents, so students must separate description from polemic.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Religious wars and persecution eventually encouraged some thinkers and governments to defend limited toleration. These policies were usually incomplete, but they influenced later arguments about conscience and religious liberty.

weeks.title: Land-Based Empires, 1450–1750
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did large empires govern religious, linguistic, and ethnic diversity?

vocabulary.gunpowder empire: A label for states whose expansion and defense used firearms and artillery, though technology alone did not explain success.
vocabulary.devshirme: An Ottoman levy that recruited some Christian boys for state and military service.
vocabulary.millet: A term often used for Ottoman arrangements granting recognized religious communities limited autonomy.
vocabulary.zamindar: A revenue intermediary or landholder in Mughal South Asia.
vocabulary.absolutism: A political doctrine or practice emphasizing concentrated monarchical authority.
vocabulary.legitimacy: Public acceptance or justification of a ruler’s right to govern.

keyUnderstandings: Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, Ming-Qing, Russian, African, and European states used different combinations of military power, taxation, religion, and local elites.
Imperial diversity was managed through negotiation as well as coercion.
Court art and architecture communicated legitimacy but should be compared with tax, legal, and local records.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Early modern land empires expanded through military organization, fiscal systems, dynastic alliances, and control of strategic routes. Gunpowder mattered, but states also needed administrators, food supplies, skilled workers, and agreements with local powerholders.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: The Ottoman Empire governed Muslims, Christians, Jews, and many language groups through layered institutions. Safavid rulers promoted Twelver Shiism as a state identity. Mughal emperors used revenue systems, military service, alliances, and changing religious policies. Ming and Qing rulers administered a vast agrarian economy, while Russia expanded across Eurasia.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Palaces, mosques, forts, paintings, ceremonies, and titles projected universal authority. Yet petitions, tax registers, and provincial records reveal bargaining and resistance. Imperial rule was often strongest near administrative centers and weaker at frontiers.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Studying several empires together prevents one-region narratives and highlights a recurring political problem: how a central government can govern diverse communities without unlimited resources.

weeks.title: Oceanic Exploration and the Columbian Exchange
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did oceanic expansion create new connections while producing conquest, demographic collapse, and ecological change?

vocabulary.maritime technology: Tools and knowledge used for navigation, shipbuilding, and ocean travel.
vocabulary.Columbian Exchange: The movement of organisms, people, diseases, and goods between hemispheres after 1492.
vocabulary.conquistador: A Spanish conqueror involved in campaigns in the Americas.
vocabulary.encomienda: A Spanish colonial grant of Indigenous labor and tribute under claimed obligations of protection and conversion.
vocabulary.ecological imperialism: Expansion aided by transferred plants, animals, pathogens, and environmental change.

keyUnderstandings: European voyages built on Afro-Eurasian navigational knowledge, commercial competition, state finance, and maritime technology.
Indigenous American societies actively negotiated, resisted, allied, and adapted during encounters.
Disease, warfare, forced labor, and ecological change produced catastrophic population losses in many regions.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Portuguese and Spanish voyages emerged from Mediterranean and Atlantic experience, African and Asian knowledge, ship design, navigation, and state-commercial competition. These voyages joined existing ocean worlds rather than creating global exchange from nothing.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: In the Americas, Europeans encountered large, politically complex societies. Conquest depended on Indigenous allies, internal rivalries, weapons, disease, and contingent decisions. Indigenous peoples were not passive, and resistance continued for centuries.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: The Columbian Exchange moved maize, potatoes, cassava, tomatoes, horses, cattle, sugar, pathogens, and people. New crops supported population growth in some regions, while disease and colonial labor systems devastated communities elsewhere.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Global connection cannot be evaluated only by the volume of trade. Historians must ask who controlled exchange, who carried the costs, and how ecological consequences reshaped daily life.

weeks.title: Atlantic Slavery, Colonialism, and Resistance
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did racial slavery become embedded in Atlantic economies, and how did enslaved people resist?

vocabulary.chattel slavery: A system treating enslaved people as legally owned property, often for life and by descent.
vocabulary.Middle Passage: The forced Atlantic voyage carrying enslaved Africans to the Americas.
vocabulary.plantation: A large agricultural enterprise relying on controlled labor to produce cash crops.
vocabulary.racialization: The process of assigning social meaning and hierarchy to perceived physical differences.
vocabulary.abolition: The movement and process of ending slavery.
vocabulary.maroon community: A community established by people who escaped slavery.

keyUnderstandings: African societies had varied relationships to slavery, but Atlantic demand expanded warfare, capture, and human trafficking.
European colonial law increasingly made slavery racial, hereditary, and permanent.
Enslaved people resisted through survival, family, culture, work slowdowns, escape, revolt, legal petitions, and abolitionist organizing.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: The Atlantic slave trade forcibly transported millions of Africans over more than three centuries. European traders, African political actors, merchants, and American plantation owners participated in a changing system, but European colonial demand and shipping networks drove its enormous expansion.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Plantation economies produced sugar, tobacco, rice, coffee, and cotton for distant markets. Colonial laws defined people as property and made status inheritable through the mother in many jurisdictions. Racial ideologies developed to justify exploitation and unequal rights.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Ship records quantify voyages but reduce people to categories. Narratives, court petitions, advertisements, songs, archaeology, and family histories restore individual experience while showing source limits. Resistance occurred every day as well as in famous rebellions.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Atlantic slavery shaped wealth, law, race, migration, foodways, music, religion, and political debate across several continents. Its legacies did not end with legal abolition.

weeks.title: Enlightenment and Political Thought
weeks.essentialQuestion: Who should hold political authority, and what rights or duties limit government?

vocabulary.natural rights: Rights understood as belonging to people by nature rather than granted solely by government.
vocabulary.social contract: A theory that political authority arises from an agreement among people or between people and rulers.
vocabulary.separation of powers: Division of government authority among institutions to reduce concentration of power.
vocabulary.popular sovereignty: The principle that legitimate political power originates with the people.
vocabulary.salon: A gathering for intellectual and social discussion, often hosted by elite women in early modern Europe.
vocabulary.public sphere: Spaces and networks in which people debate matters of common concern.

keyUnderstandings: Enlightenment thinkers debated sovereignty, rights, religious toleration, law, economy, and human nature rather than sharing one program.
Print culture, salons, coffeehouses, scientific societies, and colonial encounters expanded political debate.
Claims of universal rights often coexisted with slavery, empire, patriarchy, and exclusions that critics exposed.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century thinkers reconsidered political authority amid religious conflict, scientific change, commercial expansion, and stronger states. Hobbes emphasized security and sovereign power; Locke defended natural rights and government by consent; Montesquieu examined divided power; Rousseau explored popular sovereignty.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Women writers, abolitionists, religious dissenters, and thinkers outside Europe challenged the limits of supposedly universal claims. Mary Wollstonecraft argued that denying education to women contradicted rational equality. Enslaved and colonized people used rights language to expose hypocrisy.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Political texts must be read as arguments, not timeless rulebooks. Students identify assumptions, intended audiences, historical problems, and terms whose meanings changed over time.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Modern constitutional systems still debate liberty, equality, security, property, representation, and the limits of majority rule. Studying competing theories helps students recognize that democratic design involves tradeoffs.

sourceStudy.title: Political Philosophers in Conversation
sourceStudy.context: Compare selections from Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Wollstonecraft, and an abolitionist voice. Identify claims about human nature and authority.

weeks.dataTask: Create an institutional diagram showing how separated powers can check one another and where deadlock may occur.
weeks.seminarPrompt: Which is the greater danger: a government too strong to restrain or too weak to protect rights?

weeks.title: Atlantic Revolutions
weeks.essentialQuestion: Why did revolutions proclaim universal principles while producing unequal outcomes?

vocabulary.revolution: A rapid and fundamental transformation in political or social order.
vocabulary.declaration: A formal public statement of principles, grievances, or independence.
vocabulary.republicanism: A political tradition emphasizing civic participation, public virtue, and government without hereditary monarchy.
vocabulary.nationalism: Political identification with a nation and the claim that it should govern itself.
vocabulary.emancipation: Legal release from slavery or another condition of unfreedom.
vocabulary.counterrevolution: A movement seeking to reverse a revolution.

keyUnderstandings: The American, French, Haitian, and Latin American revolutions influenced one another but arose from distinct social structures.
Rights declarations became tools for groups excluded by original revolutionary settlements.
The Haitian Revolution was the most successful large-scale revolt of enslaved people and transformed Atlantic politics.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Atlantic revolutions grew from fiscal crisis, imperial conflict, Enlightenment arguments, local grievances, social inequality, and political organization. The American Revolution challenged British rule while preserving slavery in much of the new republic. The French Revolution attacked privilege and monarchy but passed through violence, war, and changing regimes.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: In Saint-Domingue, enslaved people transformed a colonial uprising into the Haitian Revolution, defeated major empires, abolished slavery, and created an independent state. Across Latin America, independence movements involved creole elites, Indigenous communities, free and enslaved people, regional rivalries, and international war.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Declarations reveal ideals, but constitutions, voting laws, property rules, and labor systems show implementation. Petitions by women, free people of color, enslaved people, and workers demonstrate how excluded groups interpreted revolutionary promises.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Revolutions expand political possibility while creating new conflicts over who belongs to the people. Their legacies are best judged through both principle and lived outcome.

weeks.title: Industrial Revolution
weeks.regions: Europe, North America, and Global Economy
weeks.essentialQuestion: Did industrialization improve human life, and for whom?

vocabulary.industrialization: The expansion of machine production, factories, and fossil-fuel energy.
vocabulary.urbanization: Growth in the proportion of people living in towns and cities.
vocabulary.division of labor: The separation of production into specialized tasks.
vocabulary.capital: Wealth or productive resources invested to generate further value.
vocabulary.labor union: An organization of workers formed to negotiate or act collectively.
vocabulary.externality: A cost or benefit imposed on people not directly included in an economic transaction.

keyUnderstandings: Industrialization depended on agriculture, capital, coal, technology, colonial trade, transport, labor, and institutions.
Factory production increased output while reorganizing time, skill, family labor, and workplace discipline.
Industrial growth raised long-run productivity but generated severe inequality, pollution, dangerous work, and urban hardship.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Industrialization began earliest in Britain through an interaction of coal, commercial agriculture, capital, colonial connections, skilled labor, transport, and patent and market institutions. Textile machinery, steam power, iron production, and railways altered production and movement.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Factories concentrated workers and machines under schedules enforced by owners and supervisors. Women and children performed essential labor, often at lower wages. Artisans faced both displacement and new opportunities. Rapid urban growth overwhelmed housing, sanitation, and public health systems.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Evidence includes factory testimony, wage books, census records, photographs, parliamentary reports, advertisements, and pollution data. Reform investigations sometimes exposed abuse while also reflecting middle-class assumptions about workers.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Industrialization should not be reduced to progress or misery. It created wealth and longer-term improvements in many places while distributing gains and harms unequally. Economic growth and human welfare must be measured with more than total production.

weeks.title: Capitalism, Socialism, Labor, and Reform
weeks.essentialQuestion: What should markets, governments, employers, workers, and communities each control?

vocabulary.capitalism: An economic system based largely on private ownership, markets, wage labor, and investment.
vocabulary.laissez-faire: The view that government should interfere minimally in economic exchange.
vocabulary.socialism: A family of ideas favoring social or public control of major productive resources and greater economic equality.
vocabulary.Marxism: A theory emphasizing class conflict, historical change, and collective ownership of production.
vocabulary.collective bargaining: Negotiation between workers acting together and employers.
vocabulary.social insurance: Public programs that spread risks such as illness, unemployment, disability, or old age.

keyUnderstandings: Capitalism and socialism contain diverse schools rather than one fixed model each.
Labor reform emerged through unions, cooperatives, political parties, religious movements, mutual aid, and government regulation.
Modern economies combine markets, public institutions, households, and nonprofit organizations in different proportions.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Adam Smith described how specialization and exchange could increase productivity, while also warning about monopoly and the effects of repetitive labor. Later advocates of laissez-faire emphasized private property and limited regulation. Industrial crises and inequality encouraged socialist, cooperative, and labor alternatives.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels argued that capitalist ownership produced class conflict and exploitation. Other socialists preferred democratic reform, cooperatives, or municipal ownership. Labor unions fought for shorter hours, safer workplaces, wages, and political rights.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Economic debates should distinguish description, prediction, and moral judgment. A source may explain how markets operate, propose an ideal system, or defend the interests of a social group.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Contemporary economies are mixed. Students learn to evaluate specific policies—minimum wages, workplace rules, public education, taxation, social insurance—rather than relying only on ideological labels.

weeks.title: Imperialism and Resistance
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did industrial power, nationalism, racism, and local collaboration shape imperial expansion and resistance?

vocabulary.imperialism: The extension of political, economic, or cultural control over other territories or peoples.
vocabulary.colonialism: Direct settlement or administration of a territory by an outside power.
vocabulary.Social Darwinism: The misuse of evolutionary concepts to justify hierarchy, racism, and imperial competition.
vocabulary.sphere of influence: An area where an outside power claims special economic or political privileges.
vocabulary.indirect rule: Colonial administration conducted partly through existing local authorities.
vocabulary.anti-imperialism: Opposition to empire based on self-determination, equality, economics, religion, or other principles.

keyUnderstandings: Industrial weapons and transport aided empire, but conquest also depended on local alliances, finance, medicine, and political divisions.
Colonial rule reorganized land, labor, borders, education, law, and trade for imperial priorities.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: In the nineteenth century, European states expanded formal control across much of Africa and Asia while the United States and Japan also built empires. Industrial production created demand for raw materials and markets, but prestige, strategy, missionary activity, and racial ideology also mattered.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Colonial regimes used direct and indirect rule, concessions, taxation, forced labor, schools, and legal categories. Borders often ignored existing political and cultural relationships. Local elites sometimes collaborated to protect influence, while others resisted or shifted strategies over time.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Imperial propaganda portrayed conquest as civilization. Anti-imperial voices exposed violence, economic extraction, hypocrisy, and cultural destruction. Photographs, maps, treaties, company records, and oral histories reveal both official claims and local experience.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Imperial legacies include borders, languages, infrastructure, economic dependency, legal systems, migration, and movements for national liberation. These outcomes were neither uniform nor inevitable.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand triggered a crisis, but war became continental and global because leaders made choices within alliance systems, military timetables, imperial rivalries, and nationalist politics. Colonized peoples supplied soldiers, labor, food, and resources.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Machine guns, artillery, submarines, poison gas, railways, and mass conscription changed warfare. Civilians faced blockade, occupation, hunger, forced migration, censorship, and propaganda. The war was fought in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and the oceans.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: In Russia, military failure and social crisis helped overthrow the monarchy. Bolsheviks promised peace, land, and worker power, then fought a civil war and built a one-party state. The revolution inspired supporters and opponents worldwide.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Peace settlements redrew borders and created mandates while often applying self-determination selectively. Wartime violence and unresolved grievances shaped later conflicts.

weeks.title: The Interwar World
weeks.essentialQuestion: Why did some societies respond to crisis with democratic reform while others turned toward authoritarian rule?

vocabulary.Great Depression: A severe global economic contraction beginning in 1929.
vocabulary.fascism: An ultranationalist authoritarian ideology rejecting liberal democracy and political pluralism.
vocabulary.Nazism: The German fascist movement centered on dictatorship, racial hierarchy, antisemitism, and expansion.
vocabulary.Stalinism: The centralized, coercive political and economic order associated with Joseph Stalin’s rule.
vocabulary.appeasement: A policy of making concessions to avoid conflict.
vocabulary.propaganda: Communication designed to shape attitudes or behavior, often selectively or emotionally.

keyUnderstandings: The Great Depression spread through interconnected finance, trade, production, and policy failures.
Authoritarian movements used crisis, propaganda, violence, nationalism, and institutional weakness to dismantle opposition.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: After World War I, many countries faced debt, unstable borders, political violence, and contested democratic institutions. The 1929 financial crash deepened into a global depression as banks failed, demand fell, trade contracted, and unemployment soared.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Fascist movements promised unity, order, national revival, and destruction of political enemies. In Germany, Nazis used elections, elite bargains, emergency powers, propaganda, terror, and racial law to create a dictatorship. In the Soviet Union, Stalin imposed forced collectivization, rapid industrialization, purges, censorship, and mass repression.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Propaganda works through repetition, emotion, symbols, selective truth, and control of alternatives. Students analyze it without reproducing dehumanizing messages uncritically. Economic data and private testimony reveal experiences that official posters conceal.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Democracies responded differently through public works, welfare expansion, coalition politics, isolation, rearmament, and accommodation. Institutional choices mattered even under severe economic pressure.

weeks.title: World War II, the Holocaust, and Genocide Studies
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did dictatorship, war, bureaucracy, racism, and individual choices make mass persecution and genocide possible?

vocabulary.genocide: Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group.
vocabulary.Holocaust: The systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators.
vocabulary.antisemitism: Prejudice, hostility, or discrimination directed against Jews.
vocabulary.ghetto: A confined urban district where Jews were forcibly concentrated under Nazi occupation.
vocabulary.collaboration: Cooperation with an occupying or oppressive power, under conditions that may vary in coercion and choice.
vocabulary.resistance: Opposition to persecution or occupation through armed, unarmed, spiritual, cultural, or rescue activity.

keyUnderstandings: The Holocaust developed through escalating exclusion, law, dispossession, deportation, occupation, and mass murder.
Nazi Germany targeted Jews for total destruction and also persecuted Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners, political opponents, LGBTQ people, and others.
Choices by institutions, officials, collaborators, bystanders, rescuers, and resisters shaped events within unequal and dangerous conditions.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: World War II grew from expansion by Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, and militarist Japan, unresolved postwar tensions, and failures of collective security. The conflict became global, involving mass mobilization, occupation, strategic bombing, forced labor, and civilian displacement.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: The Holocaust was not an accidental byproduct of war. Nazi racial ideology and antisemitism were translated into laws, bureaucratic procedures, property seizure, ghettos, shootings, deportations, forced labor, and killing centers. War created opportunities for radicalization, but people and institutions made choices at each stage.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Survivor testimony, laws, photographs, diaries, transport records, perpetrator documents, artifacts, and trial evidence must be studied carefully. Ethical teaching avoids simulations that ask students to pretend to be victims or perpetrators. It centers human beings and precise evidence.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Genocide study asks how identity, propaganda, law, institutions, war, and dehumanization interact. It also teaches that prevention depends on accurate warning, protected rights, accountable institutions, and action before mass violence reaches its final stages.

weeks.title: The Cold War
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did a rivalry between superpowers become a worldwide political, military, economic, and cultural system?

vocabulary.Cold War: A prolonged global rivalry led by the United States and Soviet Union without direct full-scale war between them.
vocabulary.containment: A strategy intended to limit the expansion of Soviet influence.
vocabulary.nuclear deterrence: The attempt to prevent attack through the threat of devastating retaliation.
vocabulary.proxy war: A conflict in which outside powers support opposing sides rather than fight one another directly.
vocabulary.nonalignment: A policy of avoiding formal alignment with major Cold War blocs.
vocabulary.détente: A period or policy of reduced tension between rival states.

keyUnderstandings: The Cold War combined ideology, security fears, nuclear weapons, alliances, economics, propaganda, and decolonization.
Conflicts in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East had local causes as well as superpower involvement.
Nonaligned states pursued their own interests and challenged a simple two-bloc interpretation.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: After World War II, the United States and Soviet Union emerged with different political-economic systems and deep mutual suspicion. Disputes over Eastern Europe, Germany, reconstruction, and atomic weapons hardened into competing alliances and security structures.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Nuclear weapons made direct superpower war potentially catastrophic. Deterrence depended on credibility, communication, and assumptions about rational behavior. Arms races coexisted with diplomacy, treaties, espionage, science, culture, and space competition.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Proxy wars were never merely pieces on a superpower chessboard. Local movements pursued independence, revolution, state-building, ethnic power, land reform, or regime survival. Outside intervention altered those conflicts but did not create every grievance.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: The Cold War ended through economic strain, reform, popular movements, nationalism within the Soviet bloc, leadership choices, and changing international conditions. Its institutions and memories continue to shape global politics.

weeks.title: Decolonization and Human Rights
weeks.essentialQuestion: How did colonized peoples transform self-determination from a promise into political movements and new states?

vocabulary.decolonization: The ending of colonial rule and creation or recovery of political sovereignty.
vocabulary.partition: The division of territory into separate political units.
vocabulary.nonviolence: Organized resistance that rejects physical violence while using protest, boycott, noncooperation, or civil disobedience.
vocabulary.apartheid: South Africa’s legally enforced system of racial classification and domination.
vocabulary.Universal Declaration of Human Rights: The 1948 United Nations statement of common human rights principles.
vocabulary.nation-building: The political and social work of building institutions, identity, and legitimacy within a state.

keyUnderstandings: Decolonization resulted from organized movements, imperial weakness, global war, international pressure, and changing ideas of legitimacy.
Independence strategies ranged from negotiation and mass nonviolence to armed struggle and international diplomacy.
New states inherited borders, economies, institutions, and conflicts shaped by colonial rule but made consequential choices of their own.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: European empires weakened during two world wars, while colonized soldiers, workers, students, veterans, women, religious leaders, and political organizations demanded self-government. India’s independence and partition, African liberation movements, Arab nationalism, and Caribbean independence followed different paths.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Nonviolent campaigns could mobilize mass participation and expose repression, while armed movements argued that colonial regimes would not leave voluntarily. In many cases, strategies overlapped. Cold War powers supported or opposed movements according to strategic interests.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights established a common standard after wartime atrocities. Anticolonial leaders used human-rights and self-determination language, but new governments faced poverty, borders drawn by empires, unequal trade, regional divisions, and institutional shortages.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Decolonization did not simply replace foreign rulers with stable nation-states. It opened ongoing debates about citizenship, language, land, minority rights, development, and historical memory.

weeks.title: Globalization, Trade, Development, and Migration
weeks.unit: Unit 8 · The Contemporary World and Civic Life
weeks.essentialQuestion: How should societies evaluate the gains, risks, and unequal effects of global interdependence?

vocabulary.globalization: Increasing cross-border connection in production, finance, information, culture, and movement.
vocabulary.supply chain: The linked stages through which a good or service is designed, produced, transported, and sold.
vocabulary.comparative advantage: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
vocabulary.development indicator: A measure used to describe economic or social conditions.
vocabulary.remittance: Money sent by migrants to people in another place, often family members.
vocabulary.sustainability: Meeting present needs while protecting long-term ecological and social capacity.

keyUnderstandings: Global production can lower prices and expand opportunity while shifting labor, environmental, and security risks across borders.
Development must be evaluated through health, education, rights, inequality, resilience, and environment as well as income.
Migration is shaped by work, family, conflict, climate, policy, networks, and individual agency.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Modern supply chains divide design, extraction, manufacturing, logistics, marketing, and finance across many countries. Container shipping, digital communication, trade agreements, and global finance reduced some transaction costs while increasing dependence on distant systems.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Comparative advantage explains why specialization can raise total output, but real trade also involves bargaining power, labor standards, strategic industries, environmental costs, and adjustment for displaced workers. Consumers may benefit from lower prices while communities bear hidden costs.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Development indicators such as income, life expectancy, schooling, inequality, and emissions answer different questions. A country can improve one measure while worsening another. Migration data must distinguish stocks, flows, refugees, internally displaced people, and temporary workers.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Globalization is neither a single force nor a yes-or-no choice. Policy determines how risks and benefits are distributed and how resilient communities are when supply chains, climate, or conflict disrupt normal exchange.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Governments organize power through constitutions, laws, offices, courts, elections, parties, and administrative institutions. Parliamentary and presidential systems distribute executive authority differently. Federal and unitary systems divide territorial power differently. No design guarantees liberty or effectiveness by itself.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Rule of law requires more than written rules. It depends on independent institutions, fair procedures, enforceable rights, transparency, and the ability to challenge officials. Authoritarian systems may hold elections or adopt constitutions while limiting meaningful competition and accountability.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Digital information environments reward attention. Misleading content may use emotional language, cropped images, false authority, fabricated citations, or genuine evidence removed from context. Generative AI can assist research but can also invent facts, sources, quotations, or images.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
